articles.title: Designing a 12-Seat Voice Room: WebRTC/SFU, Server-Authoritative Coins, and Moderation
articles.excerpt: Social voice rooms look simple: a grid of 10–12 mic seats, a chat strip, some gift animations. Underneath, they combine three hard problems — real-time media, money, and trust & safety. Get any one wr…
articles.body: Social voice rooms look simple: a grid of 10–12 mic seats, a chat strip, some gift animations. Underneath, they combine three hard problems — real-time media, money, and trust & safety. Get any one wrong and the room either lags, leaks money, or turns toxic. This post walks through a practical design for a multi-seat voice room: how to route audio, how to keep a virtual-coin economy honest, and how to build moderation into the architecture instead of bolting it on. 1. Media: why an SFU, not mesh or MCU With WebRTC you have three topologies: Mesh (P2P): every participant sends to every other participant. With 12 speakers, each client uploads 11 streams. Mobile uplinks and batteries give up fast. Fine for 1:1 or 3-person calls, not for rooms.

articles.title: The five editing passes I run before anyone else reads the page
articles.excerpt: Most people edit by rereading. Rereading catches typos. It does not catch why the page isn't working. I edit prose for other people, in English and French. I only ever run five passes, one problem eac…
articles.body: Most people edit by rereading. Rereading catches typos. It does not catch why the page isn't working. I edit prose for other people, in English and French. I only ever run five passes, one problem each, in this order. I don't mix them, because each pass is blind to the others. 1. The claim pass. Read only the first sentence of every paragraph. If those sentences don't form an argument on their own, the structure is broken, not the prose. Fix the order before you touch a single word. Line editing a page with a crooked spine is wasted work. 2. The cut pass. Delete the first and last paragraph of every section. Most drafts open with a warm-up and close by repeating what you just said. Both are the writer clearing their throat.

articles.title: Why Instagram labels your real photo "AI info" (and how to see the metadata behind it)

articles.body: You take a real photo, remove a stray object with a generative fill tool, post it, and Instagram adds "AI info" under your name. The picture is 99% camera, but the label says otherwise. The label usually isn't about the pixels. It's about metadata the editing tool wrote into the file. Once you know where it lives, you can see it in seconds, and remove it without touching the image. What the platforms read Meta has said it labels images using industry-standard signals in the file. Two of them do most of the work: 1. C2PA Content Credentials. A signed manifest embedded in the file (in a JPEG it sits in APP11 segments as JUMBF boxes).

articles.title: NASA Tests Dual Mode Propulsion CubeSat Ahead of Launch
articles.excerpt: Spacecraft propulsion traditionally relies on volatile fuels and separate, bulky systems for different types of maneuvering in space. NASA is working to change that paradigm. Engineers at NASA’s Marsh…
articles.body: Spacecraft propulsion traditionally relies on volatile fuels and separate, bulky systems for different types of maneuvering in space. NASA is working to change that paradigm. Engineers at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, recently completed a rigorous series of environmental and physical tests on a new small satellite designed to make spaceflight safer and more efficient. The ASCENT (Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic) Propulsion Dual Mode mission is a flight demonstration of a spacecraft about the size of a large shoebox. articles.title: Hubble Spots Chaotic Secret in Galaxy
articles.excerpt: A chaotic secret hides within this seemingly serene image of spiral galaxy NGC 4698 taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and released on Sept. 18, 2026. As a spiral galaxy like our own Milky Way gal…
articles.body: ESA/Hubble & NASA, D. Thilker, the MAUVE-HST Team A chaotic secret hides within this seemingly serene image of spiral galaxy NGC 4698 taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and released on Sept. 18, 2026. As a spiral galaxy like our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disk of stars, gas, and dust. These arms are marked by opaque clumps of brown dust and dotted with small collections of bright blue stars. Unlike many other spiral galaxies, NGC 4698’s delicate spiral arms are only prominent in the outer reaches of the disk; spiral arms often wind down to the very center of a galaxy, but NGC 4698’s spiral arms appear to shy away from its glowing center. The arms instead hover in a ring-like structure around the perimeter of the galaxy.
